distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer clinical disease leaf for uterine infection complicating pregnancy loss or pregnancy termination before fetal viability. Spontaneous, medical, surgical, unsafe, retained-products, post-instrumentation, clostridial, streptococcal, gram-negative, hemorrhagic, shock, DIC, endocarditis, and source-control-failure presentations remain mechanisms, axes, risk/context modifiers, event hazards, treatment modifiers, or future subtype layers rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking may consume recent pregnancy loss or abortion context, fever or hypothermia, pelvic/lower abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or discharge, uterine or pelvic tenderness, retained products of conception on ultrasound, systemic inflammatory labs, shock physiology, coagulopathy, and source-control need. Culture species, susceptibility, operative/pathology confirmation, treatment response, hysterectomy pathology, ECMO course, and follow-up outcome remain confirmatory or non-ranking unless a post-workup mode explicitly consumes them.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Recent abortion or pregnancy loss is the defining source context for septic abortion.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Retained products and necrotic decidual nidus
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Retained products of conception, infected clot, necrotic decidua, or malodorous intrauterine tissue maintain microbial growth and prevent full source resolution.

Genital, enteric, anaerobic, streptococcal, staphylococcal, gram-negative, and less common respiratory or clostridial organisms can infect the endometrium, myometrium, retained tissue, blood, or peritoneal fluid.

Neutrophilic infection of endometrium, myometrium, tubes, pelvic peritoneum, or adjacent tissues produces pelvic pain, cramping, uterine tenderness, abnormal bleeding, discharge, cervical findings, peritoneal signs, and imaging inflammation.
Septic abortion ranges from fever and rigors to shock and organ dysfunction.

Toxin-producing clostridial uterine infection can cause leukemoid reaction, capillary leak, third spacing, refractory shock, hemoconcentration, myonecrosis or necrotic uterus, severe organ failure, and sometimes minimal fever.
DIC and hemorrhage are optional but important severe septic-abortion complications.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Bacteremia, metastatic seeding, and organ dysfunction
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Uterine-source bacteremia and severe sepsis can seed valves, joints, lungs, peritoneum, or soft tissues and can cause AKI, ARDS, encephalopathy, septic arthritis, endocarditis, or abscess complications.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Active antimicrobial coverage and uterine source-control resolution
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Concordant broad-spectrum antimicrobial exposure plus uterine evacuation, repeat evacuation, drainage, or hysterectomy when needed reshapes the trajectory toward microbial clearance and resolving inflammation.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Pregnancy loss or termination can leave retained gestational tissue, clot, or necrotic decidua.
Open cervix, bleeding tissue, or instrumentation allows ascent or inoculation of genital and enteric organisms.
Retained or necrotic tissue sustains microbial burden.
Intrauterine microbial burden produces endometrial, myometrial, and pelvic inflammation.
Uterine and pelvic infection can trigger systemic inflammatory response and sepsis.
High bacterial burden or bacteremia can quickly drive sepsis physiology.
Clostridial uterine infection is a subset of anaerobic burden that can produce toxin-mediated shock.
Sepsis and shock activate coagulation and fibrinolytic cascades.
Toxin-mediated shock can accelerate thrombocytopenia, capillary leak, and DIC-like coagulopathy.
Sepsis and bacteremia increase metastatic infection and organ dysfunction risk.
Active broad-spectrum antimicrobials reduce susceptible uterine microbial burden.
Evacuation or operation removes retained tissue and necrotic source material.
Toxin-suppressive antibiotics and decisive source control reduce ongoing toxin production.
Recent abortion or pregnancy loss is a direct source-context observation.
Positive pregnancy test or current/recent gestation anchors the obstetric context.
Gestational age structures source-control and hemorrhage risk context.
Passage of tissue is common in incomplete abortion or septic abortion presentation.
Retained products are the observed imaging or procedural correlate of retained gestational tissue.
Echogenic intrauterine material on ultrasound can represent retained products, clot, or infected tissue.
Malodorous products are a direct source finding for infected retained tissue.
Uterine and pelvic inflammation produces pelvic pain.
Uterine infection commonly localizes to the lower abdomen.
Pelvic infection, peritonitis, or shock can present as broader abdominal pain.
Incomplete abortion and infected uterine tissue commonly cause vaginal bleeding or spotting.
Endometritis or cervicitis can produce abnormal discharge, though discharge can be absent.
Foul or tan-brown discharge suggests infected uterine contents or necrotic tissue.
Endometritis, myometritis, and retained infected tissue produce uterine tenderness.
Pelvic exam tenderness reflects inflamed uterus, cervix, adnexa, or peritoneum.
Cervical movement can transmit traction to inflamed uterine and pelvic tissues.
Open cervix is common during incomplete abortion or recent uterine evacuation.
Severe uterine infection, pelvic peritonitis, perforation, or ascites can cause guarding or rebound.
Septic abortion often causes fever, but toxin-mediated or immunologically blunted presentations can be afebrile.
Fever, pain, bleeding, and sepsis raise heart rate.
Pain, metabolic stress, sepsis, or acidosis increase respiratory rate.
Septic vasodilation, capillary leak, and hemorrhage lower arterial pressure.
Most cases show leukocytosis; severe sepsis may show leukopenia, and clostridial toxin can cause leukemoid reaction.
CRP rises with uterine infection and systemic inflammation.
PCT can rise markedly with bacterial sepsis and shock.
Clostridial toxic shock can produce extreme leukocytosis.
Toxin injury increases vascular permeability, ascites, pleural effusions, edema, and fluid requirements.
Clostridial infection and uncontrolled sepsis can lead to necrotic uterus or gangrenous salpingitis.
DIC consumes platelets while milder inflammation can cause reactive thrombocytosis.
DIC and liver/shock effects may prolong INR.
Coagulopathy and uterine source manipulation increase bleeding hazard.
Persistent bacteremia can seed heart valves.
Bacteremia can seed joints or periarticular tissue.
Severe uterine infection raises shock transition risk.
Shock, nephrotoxins, and sepsis raise AKI risk.
Sepsis, capillary leak, and fluid resuscitation can produce respiratory failure.
Shock, bacteremia, DIC, and organ dysfunction determine near-term survival.
Rigors severity follows bacteremia and systemic inflammatory activity.
Uterine and pelvic inflammation drives lower abdominal pain severity.
Pregnancy loss source context commonly produces vaginal bleeding.
DIC and uterine-source hemorrhage amplify vaginal bleeding severity.
Severe septic abortion can trigger DIC.
Systemic sepsis activity drives septic shock severity.

axes.shape_free_text: Recent spontaneous abortion, medical abortion, surgical abortion, passage of pregnancy tissue, or uterine evacuation context.
axes.clinical_interpretation: Recent pregnancy termination or loss is the defining source context.

axes.shape_free_text: Current or very recent pregnancy context by test, gestational sac, or obstetric history.
axes.clinical_interpretation: Current or recent pregnancy anchors the septic-abortion source context.

axes.shape_free_text: Gestational age at pregnancy loss or termination.
axes.required_context_rationale: This disease manifold requires active pregnancy or postpartum/peripartum context; without that context, nonspecific abdominal pain, hypertension, hemolysis, liver injury, fever, or shock should not make it rank high.

BUN reflecting hydration, renal perfusion, kidney injury, or catabolic state.
INR as a coagulation axis in sepsis, DIC, liver dysfunction, or dilution.

Tenderness over the uterus or fundus on abdominal or bimanual examination.
Diffuse pelvic tenderness on bimanual or pelvic examination.
Pain elicited by cervical motion during pelvic exam.
Abnormal vaginal discharge in the abortion or postabortal setting.
Foul, tan-brown, or malodorous discharge or blood suggesting infected uterine contents.
Open or fingertip-dilated cervical os during incomplete abortion or recent evacuation.
Abdominal tenderness from pelvic infection, uterine tenderness, or peritonitis.
Guarding, rebound tenderness, or peritoneal irritation.
Ultrasound, CT, procedural, or pathology evidence of retained products of conception.
Echogenic or thick material in the endometrial cavity.
Thickened or hyperemic endometrium on ultrasound in the postabortal setting.
Malodorous intrauterine products, necrotic decidua, or infected clot at evacuation.
Pelvic free fluid, ascites, or inflammatory fluid in the pelvis.
Intrauterine gas, uterine wall gas, or free air suggesting gas-forming infection, instrumentation, or perforation context.
Extreme leukocytosis pattern, especially WBC above roughly 30-50 x10^9/L in toxin-mediated disease.
Edema, ascites, pleural effusions, large positive fluid balance, or shock from vascular leak.
Need for uterine evacuation, repeat evacuation, drainage, or definitive operative source control.
axes.clinical_interpretation: Retained infected tissue or uncontrolled uterine source frequently creates source-control need.

axes.shape_free_text: Adequacy of uterine evacuation, necrotic-tissue removal, drainage, hysterectomy, or source resolution.
Feasibility and safety of suction curettage, manual vacuum aspiration, or D&C as uterine source control.
Probability that the antimicrobial regimen covers likely or proven uterine-source organisms.
Probability that the antimicrobial regimen covers anaerobic genital and enteric organisms.
Probability that treatment includes toxin-suppressive coverage such as clindamycin when clostridial or streptococcal toxic shock is suspected.
History of severe immediate or severe delayed beta-lactam reaction affecting broad postabortal antimicrobial selection.
Need to adjust renally cleared antibiotics or avoid nephrotoxic exposure in AKI/CKD/shock contexts.
Hazard of hypotensive septic shock or vasopressor-requiring shock.
Hazard of disseminated intravascular coagulation during septic abortion.
Hazard of major uterine, procedural, intra-abdominal, or coagulopathic bleeding.
Hazard of acute kidney injury from shock, sepsis, nephrotoxins, or rhabdomyolysis.
Hazard of acute respiratory distress syndrome or hypoxic respiratory failure during severe sepsis.
Hazard of infective endocarditis from persistent uterine-source bacteremia.
Hazard of septic arthritis or metastatic joint infection from bacteremia.
Hazard of necrotic uterus, gangrenous myometritis, or uterine tissue requiring definitive operative source control.
Disease-specific lifespan mortality hazard from septic abortion, dominated by shock, DIC, hemorrhage, clostridial toxin physiology, source-control delay, and organ failure.

axes.clinical_interpretation: Rigors severity reflects systemic bacteremia/sepsis intensity in septic abortion.
Vaginal bleeding is common around abortion or pregnancy-loss source events.
Bleeding severity varies from mild bleeding to hemorrhage when septic abortion is complicated by DIC or retained tissue.
Lower abdominal pain severity reflects infected uterine source and pelvic inflammation.
Septic abortion can range from no shock to profound septic shock.
DIC is an optional severe septic-abortion complication.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Recent abortion context and retained products often co-occur but neither should be a hard diagnostic label.
Retained products increase the need for evacuation or repeat source control.
Echogenic material is a satellite of the retained-products parent finding.
Pelvic and uterine tenderness are related exam outputs but can be incomplete.
Bleeding and tissue passage commonly coexist during incomplete abortion.
Malodor is a satellite descriptor of abnormal discharge or infected blood.
Fever, pain, bleeding, and sepsis commonly raise pulse.
WBC and CRP often rise together, but severe sepsis and toxin syndromes can break the pattern.
Extreme WBC elevation maps to the leukemoid pattern axis.
Hypoperfusion tends to increase lactate when shock progresses.
Shock and vasopressor physiology increase AKI hazard.
DIC increases clinically important bleeding hazard.
Major bleeding or massive transfusion worsens short-term survival.
Septic shock is the dominant near-term mortality driver.
Adequate evacuation or operation lowers ongoing source-driven mortality hazard.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Benefit depends on active coverage of likely organisms.
Anaerobic genital and enteric flora are central to severe septic abortion.
Antibiotics do not remove retained products or necrotic uterus.

side_effects.interpretation: Gentamicin toxicity risk increases with shock or renal impairment.

treatments.context_specific_role: Broad uterine-source coverage vector with anaerobic and toxin-suppression activity while source control is arranged.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam covers many anaerobic and gram-negative uterine-source pathogens.
Clindamycin suppresses protein synthesis and toxin production when clostridial or streptococcal toxic shock is suspected.
Severe beta-lactam reaction limits use.

treatments.context_specific_role: Broad severe pelvic sepsis vector with toxin-suppression add-on when clostridial or streptococcal toxic shock is plausible.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe shock lowers tolerance for narrow or inactive empiric coverage.
This lane helps only if broader coverage matches the pathogen and susceptibility context.

treatments.context_specific_role: Escalation vector when critical illness, resistant gram-negative probability, or early regimen mismatch threatens active coverage.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Evacuation directly removes retained infected products.
Anatomic, gestational-age, perforation, or bleeding context may make simple evacuation insufficient or unsafe.
Coagulopathy or hemorrhage modifies procedure risk.

side_effects.interpretation: Evacuation can trigger bleeding, especially with DIC, higher gestational age, or adherent tissue.

treatments.context_specific_role: Source-control vector for retained products, open cervix with infected tissue, persistent uterine source, or septic incomplete abortion.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Persistent source after initial evacuation increases value of repeat source assessment.
Peritoneal signs raise concern for spread, perforation, or necrotic source beyond simple RPOC.

treatments.context_specific_role: Second-look source-control vector when initial evacuation is incomplete, imaging remains abnormal, bacteremia persists, or peritonitis/free air requires source assessment.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Necrotic or gangrenous uterus cannot be sterilized reliably with antibiotics alone.
Refractory shock with uterine source increases value of decisive operation.
Coagulopathy changes operative risk and requires support.

side_effects.interpretation: Emergency hysterectomy in septic or coagulopathic patients can cause major bleeding.

treatments.context_specific_role: Definitive source-control vector for necrotic uterus, persistent bacteremia/source failure, clostridial toxic shock with deterioration, or life-threatening uterine infection.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Extreme leukocytosis and shock increase suspicion for toxin-mediated physiology.
IVIG cannot remove infected tissue or necrotic uterus.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunctive vector only when toxic shock physiology is plausible; it remains dependent on antibiotics and source control.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Shock physiology increases benefit of fluids, vasopressors, monitoring, and ICU support.
Resuscitation supports physiology but does not sterilize or evacuate the source.

side_effects.interpretation: Large-volume resuscitation can worsen pulmonary edema or ARDS in capillary leak states.

treatments.context_specific_role: Physiologic support while antimicrobial and uterine source-control vectors address the cause.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: DIC requires correction of consumptive coagulopathy while the uterine source is controlled.
Blood products do not remove the infection trigger.

side_effects.interpretation: Blood product and crystalloid exposure can worsen third spacing in capillary leak states.

treatments.context_specific_role: Supportive vector for DIC, anemia, active bleeding, or procedural bleeding risk during source control.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Symptom control without reassessment can mask worsening peritonitis or source failure.

treatments.context_specific_role: Supportive vector with serial examination and escalation if pain, bleeding, fever, or shock persists.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Retained products are a core uterine-source context.
Retained infected tissue increases evacuation pressure.
Uncontrolled retained products sustain sepsis and mortality hazard.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises uterine-source anchoring and shifts treatment dynamics toward evacuation plus antibiotics.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Recent abortion context defines the source window.
Mucosal disruption and open cervix facilitate ascent or inoculation.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises prior and early microbial-burden activity without using procedure type as a disease-name qualifier.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Delay allows uterine infection to progress to systemic sepsis.
Delayed adequate therapy increases bacteremia and metastatic seeding risk.
Delay worsens shock and source-control outcomes.

present.trajectory_modulation: Prolongs high-burden disease until active coverage and source control are achieved.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Gestational age affects bleeding and evacuation complexity.
Higher tissue burden and bleeding increase hemorrhage risk.
Later gestation or heavy bleeding can complicate evacuation and source control.

present.trajectory_modulation: Shifts toward mixed septic-hemorrhagic physiology and procedural support needs.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Toxin-producing pathogens reshape the trajectory toward leukemoid shock and capillary leak.
Extreme WBC response supports toxin phenotype.
Toxin shock carries high mortality when source control is delayed.

present.trajectory_modulation: Activates toxin-suppression and decisive source-control semantics without making clostridial infection the disease name.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Unusual pathogens and resistance can make common empiric regimens inactive.
Inactive coverage prolongs systemic response.

present.trajectory_modulation: Treats susceptibility as external context that modulates coverage rather than a semantic disease label.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Fever can be absent despite severe infection.
Lower physiologic reserve raises shock risk.
Comorbidity increases kidney vulnerability during sepsis or nephrotoxic therapy.

present.trajectory_modulation: Can blunt classic inflammatory signs while increasing complication and treatment-toxicity risk.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Nonsterile instrumentation and delayed access increase polymicrobial burden.
Trauma, retained tissue, or delayed care increase source-control pressure.
Unsafe procedures and delayed care increase severe outcomes.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises microbial-burden and source-control-risk context without putting unsafe abortion in the disease name.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Inadequate evacuation or persistent necrotic tissue sustains the source.
Uncontrolled source sustains shock physiology.
Source-control delay is a major mortality driver.

present.trajectory_modulation: Keeps microbial, inflammatory, and toxin fields active until source control improves.

risk_factors.clinical_rationale: Second-trimester spontaneous abortion provides the defining uterine source context for septic abortion.
Shock at transfer supports severe septic-abortion physiology when an abortion source is present.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Pre-DIC context lowers expected platelet count.
Coagulopathy context raises bleeding hazard.
Severe uterine infection raises source-control need.

risk_factors.clinical_rationale: Pre-DIC laboratory context supports the DIC/bleeding complication geometry of septic abortion.

supportive_care: Structure obstetric context directly: positive pregnancy test, gestational age, recent pregnancy loss or termination, passage of tissue, open cervical os, and retained products are observed context/source axes, not diagnosis labels.

Use parent finding plus satellite structure for RPOC and discharge: retained_products_of_conception_presence is the parent; endometrial echogenic material, hyperemia, and malodorous products are child/satellite axes. vaginal_discharge_activity is the parent for malodorous discharge.

Keep postpartum endometritis, PID without RPOC, tubo-ovarian abscess, ectopic pregnancy, toxic shock syndrome, sepsis/DIC, appendicitis, diverticulitis, and urinary or pelvic mimics competitive when their observed axes are present.

Use ultrasound or CT evidence available at presentation: retained products, endometrial thickening or hyperemia, open cervical os, pelvic free fluid, intrauterine gas/free air, peritoneal signs, and source-control need can be rankable.

Culture species, susceptibility, MALDI-TOF identification, operative findings, hysterectomy pathology, post-evacuation improvement, ECMO course, and final paper diagnosis should remain confirmatory or post-workup evidence for presentation-only tests.

Source control is a state variable: antibiotics reshape microbial burden, but retained products, necrotic uterus, perforation, persistent bacteremia, clostridial toxic shock, hemorrhage, and ongoing shock determine whether evacuation, repeat procedure, or hysterectomy changes RMST.

Clostridial or streptococcal toxic shock should be represented through toxin mechanism activity, leukemoid reaction, capillary leak, shock, and source-control axes rather than as a separate disease-name qualifier inside this first-layer leaf.
DIC and hemorrhage enter outcome through event hazard axes and blood-product support, not through a hard-coded fatality rule.
quality_notes: Unique derived hazard axis is mortality_hazard_in_D-SEPTIC-ABORTION.

Septic abortion was distilled from the disease name alone; retained products, medical/surgical/unsafe context, organism, shock, DIC, and toxic shock are represented as mechanisms, axes, modifiers, or event hazards.
No treatment priority-label fields are used.
New uterus/RPOC axes should receive horizontal ontology review when postpartum endometritis, ectopic pregnancy, additional PID/TOA variants, and septic pelvic thrombophlebitis leaves are integrated.
